This page corresponds to the precise U.S. O*NET/SOC 25-1125.00 occupation "History Teachers, Postsecondary" (postsecondary history teachers): teaching courses in human history and historiography at postsecondary institutions, covering both positions primarily engaged in teaching and those combining teaching and research. Official scope text: Teach courses in human history and historiography. Includes both teachers primarily engaged in teaching and those who do a combination of teaching and research. The U.S. wage percentiles on this page come from the precise occupation data for 25-1125.00 presented by O*NET, and the employment outlook uses the U.S. postsecondary teachers parent scope; mainland China's teaching qualification and professional conduct requirements are labeled separately under their own jurisdictional sources, and the two must not be applied to each other.

To judge whether to enter postsecondary history teaching, first run one verifiable teaching task using public or simulated materials: choose a clear historical topic (for example, the impact of a country's industrialization on its social structure), complete a two-hour course design that spells out the teaching objectives, historical sources and reading materials, lecture and discussion segments, one formative assessment, and grading points; then record a 10-minute explanation or organize a peer discussion and keep a record of it. Afterward, check: whether the chosen sources can support the argument, whether historical fact and interpretation are stated separately, whether the assessment criteria are reviewable, and whether the discussion leaves evidentiary room for different positions. Finally, mark which matters fall beyond your individual teaching authorization (ruling on grade disputes, determining academic misconduct, degree conferral, admissions) and, following institutional rules, explain to whom they should be escalated. Test with a real deliverable, not just answers to an interest questionnaire.

Fit signals | The work activity importance ratings for U.S. O*NET 25-1125.00 show that identifying objects, actions, and events (95), getting information (94), updating and using relevant knowledge (92), analyzing data or information (91), and training and teaching others (90) are the most important activities for this occupation; work context shows that deciding tasks, priorities, and goals 94% report a lot of freedom, decision freedom 94% report a lot of freedom, electronic mail 86% report every day, indoors, environmentally controlled 92% report every day, face-to-face discussions 48% report every day and 48% report once a week or more, typical work week 72% report more than 40 hours, importance of being exact or accurate 45% report extremely important, public speaking 24% report every day and 76% report once a week or more, and contact with others 43% report constant contact. The most important skills are speaking (88), reading comprehension (81), learning strategies (78), writing (78), and active listening (75). If you are willing to check historical sources and interpretations over the long term, turn research into teachable courses and feedback, and accept a working style centered on reading and writing, public expression, and periodic grading, these daily demands are closer to the way you work.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows (25-1125.00): competition 38% report extremely competitive and 38% report highly competitive; typical work week 72% report more than 40 hours; time pressure 18% report every day and 54% report once a week or more; public speaking 24% report every day; importance of being exact or accurate 45% report extremely important. This occupation centers on historical sources, historiographical methods, courses, and student work; a single distorted source citation, a single conflation of fact and interpretation, or a single inconsistency in grading standards can affect teaching credibility and student rights. On the mainland China side, a postsecondary teaching credential is a separate category, determined by the competent education administrative department or an authorized institution, and it cannot be obtained merely from a degree or a job offer (Teacher Qualification Regulations and their implementation measures); at the same time, the Ten Guidelines for Professional Conduct of College Teachers in the New Era set professional conduct baselines for teaching, academic activity, and relationships with students. On the U.S. side, the broad postsecondary teachers category is projected to grow 7% from 2025 to 2035 (parent scope). If you find it hard to sustain over the long term a work rhythm centered on reading and writing, public expression, and a competitive academic market, or are unwilling to take responsibility for source accuracy and grading fairness, you should treat these as real costs that need careful weighing.

Commitment judgment | Real fit comes from whether you can do three things in the same course at once: make the teaching solid (complete lecturing, discussion, assessment, and records based on course objectives and historical sources, producing reviewable course materials, grading criteria, and feedback); keep academic standards and the boundaries of power under control (distinguish historical fact from interpretation, use others' work according to citation standards, and handle grades, academic misconduct determinations, and student information under institutional rules); and carry definable position responsibility (be responsible for your own course content and assessment, while referring matters beyond teaching authorization, such as admissions, degree conferral, and disciplinary action, to the appropriate body or committee under institutional rules). It is recommended to test this with one verifiable experience (completing a course design and grading points, a short explanation or an organized discussion, or a review of how you judged a source controversy), rather than relying only on the conclusions of an interest questionnaire.

The daily work of a postsecondary history teacher can be broken down along three lines: (1) course teaching—course design, lecturing, discussion organization, and learning assessment; (2) research and writing—gathering and critiquing sources in a specific historical field, forming interpretations, and producing papers or monographs; (3) student advising and academic service—answering questions, supervising theses or internships, and taking part in departmental curriculum and committee affairs. The three lines share the same set of source criticism and argumentation methods, but their deliverables and evaluation methods differ: teaching is delivered to students and the teaching institution, research is delivered to academic peers, and advising and service face individual students and departmental operations. The time split across these three lines varies greatly between teaching-focused positions and those that combine teaching and research.

paragraphs: Conclusion | The difference between this occupation (U.S. SOC 25-1125.00 Postsecondary History Teachers) and adjacent directions centers on "work object and deliverable audience": this occupation turns historical sources, historiographical methods, and historical interpretation into postsecondary courses, instructional training, and learning assessment, and is responsible for students' historical thinking ability; historians are primarily driven by producing historical research, and teaching is not their core deliverable; other postsecondary social science teachers use their own discipline's evidence types and analytical frameworks. These directions differ in qualifications, responsibilities, and evaluation methods, and cannot be swapped based only on job title.

Evidence note | The comparison subjects in the table below come from the O*NET occupational classification and public official materials, and are intended to help distinguish the work content and fit choices of adjacent occupations; they do not constitute conclusions about qualifications, hiring, or pay. Wages, employment, and qualifications for each occupation must be checked separately under its own SOC scope and jurisdiction; this table does not compare values numerically and does not use one occupation's wage as a proxy for another; authority over matters such as degree conferral, grade disputes, and academic misconduct determinations is governed by institutional rules.

Introduction | The comparison below is organized in four columns: "career direction—core work and outputs—key differences—what choice suits whom better". Directions such as history, anthropology and archaeology, area and ethnic studies, economics, and geography often connect within the same department in higher education, but connection does not mean they can substitute for one another; when choosing across directions, one should newly learn that discipline's evidence types, method training, and academic standards.

Key difference | This occupation takes historical sources, historiographical methods, and historical interpretation as its object; its outputs are teachable courses, learning assessment, and academic results, and it is responsible for students' training in historical thinking; other directions have their own core evidence and problem domains, for example historians focus on research output and non-teaching positions are not responsible for courses and grades.

Better suited to people who are willing to turn research into teaching, can check sources and interpretations over the long term, and are willing to take responsibility for grading fairness and academic standards for students.

Core work and outputs | Preparing course materials and readings (task importance 92), teaching historical topics (91), organizing classroom discussions (91), keeping up with developments in the field (90), conducting and publishing research (89), and constructing and grading examinations and student work (86/85); outputs are syllabi and lecture notes, classroom activity and assessment records, and academic papers or monographs.
This occupation: Postsecondary History Teachers (History Teachers, Postsecondary, 25-1125.00)

Key difference | Historians identify professionally with historical research, their main outputs are academic results and professional judgment, and they usually do not bear teaching responsibilities such as course design, student assessment, and grade records; this occupation, by contrast, must divide time between teaching and (depending on the position) research, and is directly responsible for teaching delivery.

Better suited to people willing to invest long term in archives and source research, who accept publication and peer review as the main form of evaluation, and who want research to dominate their work; this occupation is better suited to people who are willing to use research for teaching and face students directly.

Core work and outputs | Designing research questions, gathering and critiquing primary sources, forming historical interpretations, and writing papers or monographs, and participating in academic conferences and peer review; outputs are research papers, monographs, reviews, and research reports.
Historians (Historians, 19-3093.00)

Key difference | This direction uses archaeological materials and ethnographic evidence to explain the origins and cultural change of human societies, and its method training (fieldwork, material culture analysis, ethnography) differs from the documentary historiography of this occupation; when both are teaching positions, course content and assessment standards are likewise based on this discipline's evidence.
Better suited to people willing to engage with fieldwork and physical evidence, who are interested in cultural evolution and material remains, and who accept this discipline's method training.

Core work and outputs | Teaching anthropology and archaeology courses, organizing field or laboratory practice, guiding students in analyzing material remains and ethnographic materials, and conducting related research; outputs are course and field practice materials, research papers, and archaeological reports.
Anthropology and Archeology Teachers, Postsecondary (Anthropology and Archeology Teachers, Postsecondary, 25-1061.00)

Key difference | This direction takes area studies, ethnic groups, and cross-cultural comparison as its object and often uses interdisciplinary evidence (linguistic, political, social, and cultural materials), with history being only one source; this occupation centers on the critique of historical sources and chronological context.

Better suited to people who are willing to take regions and ethnic groups as long-term units of study, can integrate materials from multiple disciplines, and are attentive to cultural identity and power relations.

Core work and outputs | Teaching area, ethnic, and cultural studies courses, organizing interdisciplinary reading and discussion, guiding student research, and producing area studies results; outputs are course materials, interdisciplinary papers, and research reports.
Area, Ethnic, and Cultural Studies Teachers, Postsecondary (Area, Ethnic, and Cultural Studies Teachers, Postsecondary, 25-1062.00)

Key difference | This direction uses economic theory and econometric analysis as its main tools, and its conclusions depend on models and data; this occupation centers on source criticism and interpretive argument, with lower demands for quantitative methods. Neither can be evaluated by the other's methodological standards.
Better suited to people who are willing to use models and statistical tools, are interested in markets and the mechanisms of economic institutions, and accept quantitative evidence as the main basis.

Core work and outputs | Teaching microeconomics and macroeconomics courses, designing problem sets and examinations, guiding students in the use of statistical and econometric tools, and conducting economic research; outputs are course and problem set materials, data analysis, and economics papers.
Economics Teachers, Postsecondary (Economics Teachers, Postsecondary, 25-1063.00)

Key difference | This direction focuses on spatial distribution, human-environment relations, and geographic processes, and commonly uses tools such as maps, remote sensing, and spatial statistics; this occupation focuses on chronological context and historical interpretation, with evidence drawn mainly from documents and archives.
Better suited to people who are willing to use maps and spatial data, are attentive to environmental and regional differences, and accept spatial analysis as the main tool.

Core work and outputs | Teaching physical and human geography courses, organizing map-based and field observation teaching, guiding students in the use of geographic information systems and spatial data, and conducting geographic research; outputs are course and map materials, spatial analysis, and geography research papers.
Geography Teachers, Postsecondary (Geography Teachers, Postsecondary, 25-1064.00)

Transition | This table places adjacent directions side by side by "work object and deliverable audience", to help you judge which combination of teaching, research, and academic service you want to invest in over the long term. Whichever direction you choose, what truly determines competence is the ability to critique historical sources or evidence, the ability to turn research into courses and assessment, the willingness to take responsibility for grading fairness and academic standards for students, and the awareness to escalate beyond individual authorization according to institutional rules; an interest questionnaire is only for raising questions and cannot replace real learning and teaching experience.

subject.name: Postsecondary History Teachers
subject.summary: Postsecondary History Teachers corresponds to the precise U.S. O*NET/SOC 25-1125.00 occupation "History Teachers, Postsecondary": teaching courses in human history and historiography at postsecondary institutions, covering both positions primarily engaged in teaching and those combining teaching and research. Official scope text: Teach courses in human history and historiography. Includes both teachers primarily engaged in teaching and those who do a combination of teaching and research. Core tasks include preparing course materials (importance 92), teaching historical topics (91), organizing classroom discussions (91), keeping up with developments in the field (90), conducting and publishing research (89), and constructing and grading examinations and student work (86/85). Common job titles include history lecturer, assistant professor, associate professor, professor, and adjunct history lecturer. The U.S. wage percentiles on this page come from the precise occupation 25-1125.00 (BLS OEWS 2025, presented via O*NET), and the employment outlook uses the parent-level postsecondary teachers scope; mainland China teaching credentials and professional conduct are labeled separately under the Teacher Qualification Regulations and their implementation measures and the Ten Guidelines for Professional Conduct of College Teachers in the New Era, and the two must not be conflated.
